questions.stem: A force is a…
questions.explanation: Every push and every pull is a force. Forces can start things moving, stop them, or change their shape.

questions.stem: Sort each action into push or pull.
questions.explanation: When you kick, press or push a pram, you push away from yourself. When you open a drawer, pull a rope or hold a kite string, you pull towards yourself.

questions.stem: Match each action to what the force does.
pairs: hitting a ball with a bat
questions.explanation: Forces can change shape, start movement, stop movement and change the way something moves.

questions.stem: A mango falls down because of ___. A ball stops on grass because of ___. A force is a push or a ___.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls things down towards the Earth. Friction slows things that rub together, such as a ball on grass.

questions.stem: Friction is a force that slows things down when they rub together.
questions.explanation: Friction happens when two surfaces rub. A ball rolls far on a smooth floor but stops quickly on rough grass.

questions.stem: We measure forces with a ___, and the unit is the ___.
questions.explanation: A forcemeter has a spring inside. The harder you pull, the more it stretches, and the reading is in newtons (N).

questions.stem: Look at the forcemeter. What force does it show?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with its pointer at 4 newtons.
questions.explanation: The pointer is at 4, so the force is 4 newtons (4 N). A forcemeter reads the size of a force.

questions.stem: This forcemeter lifts a bag and shows 7 N. A second bag shows 4 N. Which bag is heavier?
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with its pointer at 7 newtons.
questions.explanation: The heavier a bag is, the more force you need to lift it, so the bigger reading belongs to the heavier bag.

questions.stem: Look at the box. How much force is needed to lift it straight up?
questions.image_alt: A box lifted straight up with a force of 10 newtons, and pulled up a ramp with a force of 4 newtons.
questions.explanation: The picture says lifting the box straight up needs 10 N. Pulling it up the ramp needs only 4 N, but the path is longer.

questions.stem: Look at the arrows on the aeroplane. Which force pulls it down towards the Earth?
questions.image_alt: An aeroplane with four arrows: lift up, weight down, thrust forward and drag backward.
questions.explanation: Weight is how hard gravity pulls on something, so the arrow pointing down is weight. The other arrows point up, forwards and backwards.

questions.stem: The forcemeter shows 7 N. If a lighter bag is hung on it, the reading will go down.
questions.image_alt: A forcemeter with its pointer at 7 newtons.
questions.explanation: A lighter bag needs less force to hold it up, so the pointer moves back towards a smaller number.

questions.stem: Motion means a change in position over time.
questions.explanation: If something is in a different place after some time, it has moved. A car that goes further in the same time is moving faster.

questions.stem: In 5 seconds toy car A goes 2 metres and toy car B goes 4 metres. Which car is moving faster?
options: they are moving at the same speed
questions.explanation: Car B goes further in the same time, so it is moving faster.

questions.stem: Why is it easier to slide on a wet, smooth floor than on a rough mat?
questions.model_answer: The smooth floor has less friction, so you slide. The rough mat has more friction.
questions.explanation: Friction is the force between two surfaces that rub. A smooth, wet floor has less of it, so things slide easily. A rough mat has more, so it slows you down.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a fair test in order to find which surface has the most friction.
sequence: Roll a toy car down a ramp onto the smooth floor.
Measure how far the car went.
Roll the same car down the same ramp onto the mat.
Measure how far it went this time.
questions.explanation: We keep the car and ramp the same and change only the surface. The surface where the car stops soonest has the most friction.

questions.stem: What can a force do to an object? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Forces can start and stop movement, change direction and change shape, such as squashing clay. A force does not change colour.

questions.stem: Kamal drives a rickshaw van. Why is it harder to pedal when the van is full of potatoes?
options: The van is heavier and needs more force.
The potatoes make the road much smoother.
Gravity stops pulling on the loaded van.
The wheels turn the wrong way round.
questions.explanation: Heavier things need more force to move. A full van has more weight, so Kamal must push the pedals harder.

questions.stem: On a wet road the van slides more when Kamal brakes. Why should he go slowly?
options: There is more friction, so it stops at once.
There is less friction, so it stops slowly.
The brakes make it go faster instead.
Gravity is weaker on wet roads here.
questions.explanation: Water makes the road slippery, so there is less friction between the tyres and the road. The van needs more space to stop.

questions.stem: Which are ways that friction helps us? Choose all that are right.
options: Shoes grip the ground so we do not slip.
A wet, smooth floor lets us slide.
A mango falls from the tree.
questions.explanation: Shoes grip because of friction, and brakes use friction to slow the wheels. Sliding on a smooth floor means very little friction, and a falling mango is gravity.

questions.stem: After rain the school corridor is wet and smooth. Sumi walks slowly because there is less friction and she could slip.
questions.explanation: A wet, smooth floor has less friction, so shoes grip less and it is easy to slip. Walking slowly is the safe choice.

questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the cart when the same-size pullers pull equally on both ropes?

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Net Force screen. Put one medium puller on the left rope and one medium puller on the right rope, then press Go.

questions.explanation: Equal pulls in opposite directions cancel each other, so the cart stays still. The side with the bigger total pull wins.

questions.stem: In the simulation, a crate you have pushed slows down and stops faster when the friction is set to lots.

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Friction screen. Push the crate so it moves, then set the push back to zero. Do this once with the friction slider on a little and once on lots.

questions.explanation: More friction means a bigger force slowing the crate. With little friction it slides much further.

questions.stem: In the simulation, with the same push, the heavy fridge speeds up more slowly than the crate.

sim.task: Open Forces and Motion: Basics and choose the Motion screen. Set friction to none. Push the crate with the applied force slider and watch its speed. Then use the same push on the fridge.

questions.explanation: A heavier object needs a bigger force to speed up. The same push makes the lighter crate speed up faster than the fridge.

questions.stem: Class 2B rolled a toy car down a ramp: smooth floor 150 cm, mat 80 cm, sand 20 cm. They now try a polished tile with even less friction than the smooth floor. What is the best prediction?
options: It goes about 80 cm, like the mat.
It goes less than 20 cm, like sand.
questions.explanation: The less friction a surface has, the further the car rolls. The smooth floor went furthest so far, so a surface with even less friction should take the car further.

questions.stem: Mina rolls a car down a tall ramp onto sand. Raju rolls the same car down a short ramp onto a smooth floor. Why is this not a fair test of friction?
options: The surfaces are different from each other.
They used the same car both times.
They did both tests in one room.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only the surface should change. A taller ramp gives the car a faster start, so the ramp must be the same height each time.

questions.stem: Tuli says, "Gravity only pulls on things that are falling." A book is lying on a table. Is Tuli right? Explain.
questions.model_answer: No. Gravity pulls on everything all the time. The book does not fall because the table holds it up.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls on every object, even when it is still. The book stays where it is because the table is in the way, so it cannot fall.
